newsitem.title: USA: SEC, U.S. attorney subpoena bond records.
newsitem.headline: SEC, U.S. attorney subpoena bond records.

text.p: Dade County Finance Director Ed Marquez said on Friday he had been subpoenaed to testify before a federal grand jury investigating corruption in the county's bond deals.
Marquez said County Manager Armando Vidal and bond administrator Lidia Monzon had also been subpoenaed to appear before the grand jury in Miami on Tuesday.
The subpoenas came one day after federal prosecutors subpoeaned records from numerous Dade County bond deals involving San Francisco-based municipal bond firm Grigsby Brandford & Co, Marquez said.

The Miami Herald reported on Thursday that FBI videotapes showed Calvin Grigsby, the former chairman of the firm, allegedly offering Dade County Commissioner James Burke a $300,000 kickback in exchange for steering a $183 million Dade County bond deal to the firm.
The conversation allegedly took place last month in a San Francisco hotel where Burke, Grigsby and Miami municipal bond firm owner Howard Gary discussed the kickbacks, the newspaper said.
The first subpoena also requested records related to the method the county uses to select bond underwriters, and records for several past and upcoming bond deals involving Grigsby Brandford.
"The inkling I got is they're going to cover the same stuff they're asking for on the other subpoenas," Marquez said of his pending grand jury appearance.
Marquez said federal investigators gave no indication how long the grand jury investigation would last.
Vidal and Monzon were not immediately available for comment Friday.
In a statement issued late Friday from Los Angeles, Grigsby's attorney said his client maintains his innocence.
"Mr. Grigsby is not in hiding or missing; nor is he being sought by authorities," said Grigsby's high-profile defense attorney, Johnnie Cochran, who successfully defended O.J. Simpson.

"There are no charges pending; and we are hopeful that no charges will be filed, because Mr. Grigsby is not only presumed innocent, but strongly maintains his innocence," Cochran said in the statement.
"You may rest assured that we will do everything within our power to see that no charges are filed; and, if they are filed, we will vigorously fight them," Cochran said.
Burke, who was chairman of the finance committee that oversees county bond issues, said the Securities and Exchange Commission had also subpoenaed documents from the finance department.
"I've encouraged them (department staff) to send more than they subpoenaed because I want to get the full story of what happened," said Burke in an interview.
Burke has denied wrongdoing and told Reuters there was no bribe. Gary, the FBI and federal prosecutors have all declined to comment.
No charges have been filed in connection with the Dade County bond allegations.

Burke, who is black, said he believes investigators were probing "primarily the minority transactions and black firms" because he has been an advocate for including minority-owned firms in bond deals.
"I've said from the rostrum that things are not going to be fair until you have inclusion of black firms, particularly at the senior level," Burke said.
Also subpoenaed were records documenting how Grigsby Brandford was chosen as senior manager for the issue.

Regarding allegations in press reports that he steered to Grigsby Brandford a $183 million revenue bond refunding for a recyling plant, Burke said the firm was selected as senior manager by the plant owner in response to an unsolicited proposal from Grigsby Brandford.
Other Dade County finance officials have said the underwriter was selected by recycling plant officials, and not by the county.

The other deal linked to the allegations, a tentative $165 million revenue bond issue for a new basketball arena, was awarded to Grigsby Brandford because they were next in line among the county's standing pool of bond underwriters, Burke said.
"It was part of our regular rotation," he said.
